412.t: Chicago jazzmen leave for New York and Hodes is left behind
412.s: The Chicago players, Condon first, went to New York and beckoned the others. Hodes stayed on, playing with Earl Wiley and others while hearing music on the South Side, even though DownBeat made New York sound paved with gold.
412.ch: Critics and the thinning Chicago scene (draft typing)
412.q: Condon went first. But one of them went first, and when he got there, waved his hand to those who were behind. Come quick, you're missing out on a fortune. And this kind of thing.

412.t: Deciding to leave Chicago for New York and marrying
412.s: Hodes says he read that New York streets were paved with gold. Accordions were taking jobs, Chicago was a ghost town, and he met his wife and made a honeymoon of the move.
412.q: Well, actually, I'd read so much about New York by this time. And all the players that were making it there, and that the streets were paved with gold. And I couldn't believe it. These guys were down here doing nothing, and I was getting lonesome. Accordions were taking all the jobs and I wasn't…

412.t: Driving to New York with his bride and two dogs
412.s: Hodes tells of packing a two-door Ford with his wife and dogs. Bill Kennedy had promised him a place to stay in New York, and he got a basement apartment.
412.q: personal belongings, hers and yours, all in the inside of that car, and you drive to New York. As that prizefighter, Bill Canady, said, Herbs, you get to New York, you got a place to stay. You belong in New York. Herbs, -- that's what they used to -- New Orleans guys. Didn't say Pops all the time,…

412.t: Dick Donahue, the stew and a lean first year
412.s: Hodes describes Chicago trumpeter Dick Donahue, who could write parts and cooked stews for musicians. His wife left for Chicago with the baby after the Christmas pork chop incident.
412.q: : Never met him before. So here we were in New York, struggling with these kind of jobs. I did know a trumpet player by the name of Dick Donahue in Chicago. We had worked at Harry's New York Bar in Chicago, or Floyd Town and His Men About Town. That was another band in Chicago that gave us work.

133.t: The 1955 drive to Manhattan: gas money, parking and hives
133.s: He and a friend arrived with about $75 each, and Walton breaks out in hives from truck fumes and has to park in the Bronx.
133.q: Yeah, I see your mind, what are you tryin' to add it up. [laughs] But no, we, we somehow we ended up in Manhattan, and I'd never heard of you can't park on this side of the … you can't, no parking. Oh, everywhere I worked, man …. And all these fumes from uh, the uh, trucks in Manhattan, you know.…

133.t: Musicians urged him to come to New York; his 1947 train trip north
133.s: Touring players kept telling him to come to New York, where he had been at thirteen by train; the trains became unsegregated at St. Louis and a Rochester family showed him a different world.
133.q: Yeah, exactly, yeah. They said, "You gotta come to New York." This … You got to uh … tryin' to remember a few others. Uh, Jerome Richardson, I remember, came through there and uh, it was a very long list of people I met and uh, whose names, names escape me. A complete list of names escape me, but…

133.t: First sight of New York and Jackie Robinson at Ebbets Field
133.s: On the 1947 trip he was amazed at Grand Central and Brooklyn, saw Jackie Robinson argue with an umpire at Ebbets Field, and he and Brower discuss Robinson's importance.
133.q: Uh, back where I'd come from, you know, but not there. And so, I arrived from Rochester down into New York, which was, which was Grand Central, and I'd never heard these words: Poughkeepsie, Utica, Schenectady. I say, "Wow, what the hell?" [laughs] Heeeeee! [laughs] [inaudible] never heard these…

133.t: Arriving in 1955 with a friend; abandoning the Manhattan School audition
133.s: Walton recalls the YMCA overnight on the drive with a friend named Milton, then planning to enroll at Manhattan School of Music but fleeing the waiting room because he was not ready.
133.q: Yeah. So we had, you know, a mutual uh, uh goal. We actually stopped off and spent the night in some city at some YMCA, you know. The budget allowed all that. I just can't believe it.

133.t: First months in New York: Sloan House YMCA, day jobs and his mother
133.s: He loved the city, lived at the 34th Street Sloan House YMCA, worked at Macy's and Horn & Hardart, and his mother told him to come home, later hearing him at Carnegie Hall.
133.q: She used to say that. Her mother said that. [chuckles] But uh, I was determined and finally, man, fast-forward, quite a while uh, uh, she was able to tell her friends that uh, she'd been to New York to hear her son play at Carnegie Hall. So that was uh, a good outcome, I think, in those who doubt…

133.t: Meeting Richie Powell and Coltrane; decision to go east
133.s: Walton recalls a brief meeting with Coltrane and a night of talk with Richie Powell about Johnny Hodges, showing how Denver gave him access to touring musicians before he drove to New York in 1955.
133.q: Yeah, very, very brief, yeah. Uh, I just went over to the table and uh, uh, you know, I had remembered his name of being on a Dizzy Gillespie record with a, people uh, names like Kansas Fields [laughs] and then John Coltrane. I started being suspicious, were these stage names or what? But they…

170.t: Blakey's telegram, leaving for New York, and the Washington engagement
170.s: Bobby Paine delivers a telegram from Art Blakey; Ware flies to New York and joins the Messengers in Washington wearing a borrowed short suit.
170.ch: Joining the Messengers and moving to New York
170.q: Anyway, they told me -- I was away somewhere, I was hanging out on 43rd Street and word got to me that Bobby Paine wanted to see me, so I went out to the Cotton Club, and he said, "Man, this is a telegram and Art Blakey wants you to come to New York." I said, "Oh my God." I didn't want to leave…

170.t: Clifford Brown's death and scuffling in New York
170.s: The Messengers lose Clifford and Richie Powell, and Ware and Ira Sullivan struggle for money in New York.
170.ch: Joining the Messengers and moving to New York
170.q: Lose Clifford and Richie Powell got killed in an automobile accident. But that was the first engagement That Art Blakey was (inaudible) beautiful, he'd tell Ira and I, "We got to scuffle and we kind of had to scuttle for ourselves now; he said he was gonna put us out on the corner of 52nd and…

170.t: Philadelphia with Lee Morgan and quitting Blakey
170.s: Ware fears Philly police over scars, meets Lee Morgan, misses a night with a toothache, and returns to New York.
170.ch: Joining the Messengers and moving to New York
170.q: Our next engagement was, let's see ... Atlantic City; our next engagement I think was Trenton. Yeah, it was Trenton, New Jersey, and then we had another engagement in Philadelphia. Now, I didn't want to go to Philly, because I had heard that the police were so tough on the addicts or people they…

170.t: Returning to New York in 1967 and Blue Mitchell at Smalls
170.s: Ware leaves Chicago before the riot, arrives in a riot-torn New York, and plays with Blue Mitchell opposite Lucky Thompson.
170.ch: Return to New York in the late 1960s
170.q: Well, anyway, I decided to come back to New York. That was around August, around July. I left Chicago just before the riot started out there, and I got to New York, where they had another riot up there in Harlem. That's when Lindsay walked the streets, you know, (unintelligible) doing all that.

170.t: Leaving Chicago in 1956: Max Roach at the Beehive
170.s: Side 2 begins; Ware recounts the Messengers visiting Chicago and Leo Blevins taking him to meet Max Roach and Clifford Brown at the Beehive.
170.ch: Joining the Messengers and moving to New York
170.q: had been in town -- I didn't catch the first, the original, group -- that was the one with Horace Mobley Donald and Hank Moby, Don Byrd, Doug Watkins, and Art Blakey Reckie -- That's the original Messengers they were the originals. They had been in, and I missed the band, and Max was working at the…

77.t: Leaving Chicago for New York and the Broadway audition
77.s: Looking for higher ground she leaves Chicago on a Wednesday and opens on Broadway on Saturday; Bill Robertson sends her to Jack Goldberg to audition with her songs.
77.q: : From Chicago, let me see. Well -- oh, from Chicago, I'll tell you how I got to Chicago. I had done everything I could do in Chicago, and I'm looking for some higher ground, you know.

77.t: Where she lived in 1920s New York
77.s: Addresses on West 136th Street and Edgecombe Avenue, with Sugar Hill and Strivers' Row.
77.q: I lived, yes, one while I lived at 233 West 136th Street. And that was Bert Williams' niece. His oldest niece and I lived there. We had the apartment. And let me see, where else did I live? Oh, 287 Edgecomb, 287 Edgecomb, we had a --

77.t: Madam Walker's Sunday house and the dicties
77.s: She went every Sunday to Walker's house on St. Nicholas Avenue, among show people such as Lottie Tyler, Edna Thomas and Jimmy Daniels, the so-called dicties.
77.q: Madam Walker was one of my best friends. I used to go to her house every Sunday. Wasn't a Sunday I didn't -- didn't miss a Sunday. Lottie Tyler, who was my girl friend, Lottie Tyler and Edna Thomas and let me see, who else, we were considered the dicties, they called us dicties, you know. We were…

77.t: Chicago versus New York; Mattie Hite urges her to go east
77.s: Chicago was always the greatest, but Mattie Hite told her she belonged in New York, so she decided to go to higher ground.
77.q: Always the greatest. It still is, I guess. Chicago was the greatest, yeah. And I tell you, you asked me how I happened to think about coming to New York, Mattie Height, a girl that was with Cora Green and them down there at the Panama, she said to me, said, 'Girl, you ain't got no business here;…

77.t: Chicago versus New York as the place to make it
77.s: Hunter insists Chicago was where you got recognized and its nightclubs never matched by New York, partly due to the gangsters.
77.ch: New Orleans musicians, recordings and radio
77.q: If you don't make it in New York, you might as well forget it. But Chicago was the place to go to get it at that time. You came to Chicago, and if -- if you came to Chicago and said you had worked in Chicago, you had been recognized in Chicago as a musician or an artist, then you were somebody. New…

409.t: Staying behind in New York when the cooperative band went home
409.s: Cootie and Edmond Hall refused to go back to Florida, and lived on dime rolls and coffee from a Brooklyn baker.
409.q: Yeah. So after the two weeks they were ready to go back. I said, "Not me." I said, "This is the place I've wanted to be all my life. I'm not thinking about going back to no Florida." And Helen, we was -- I was with the biggest band in the State of Florida. Colored band. And during that time, it was…

409.t: Living with Chick Webb and Trueheart
409.s: Chick Webb took him under his wing, in rooms across from the Bandbox shared with guitarist Trueheart.
409.q: Yeah. It was a In the musicians' house. There wasn't nobody staying there but musicians.

409.t: Hired for the Rosemont Ballroom and the trip to New York
409.s: The owner of the Rosemont Ballroom in Brooklyn heard the radio broadcasts and hired the band; they came north by boat from Georgia.
409.q: Because, Helen, when I used to say my prayers at night, I used to say, "Dear Lord, please hurry up and let me grow up so I can get to New York."

409.t: Trumpet night at the Bandbox and Chick Webb takes him in
409.s: Told to try the Bandbox jam sessions, he played trumpet night, and Chick Webb came, paid his landlady and took him in.
409.q: That was our dinner. So we don't know -- so we run into some people and they say, "So what are you guys doing?" A musician, I think, one of the guys was. "They ain't doing nothing, man." "We need a job." Said, "Why don't you all go over to New York?" We said, "We're in New York."

95.t: Going to New York to record, six-month stays
95.s: She went to New York to record in 1924 and 1925, staying six or seven months each time though her brother objected.
95.ch: Friends, New York life and recording routine

But Mr. ________ told me in New York City, told me, said, anytime I come to record, always bring some of George's songs because George was the one that made you acquainted with us. But my brother didn't know that, but he (unintelligible) number to record ________.…

95.t: Cooking for herself in New York
95.s: She cooked steak, rice, greens and cornbread wherever she had a stove.
95.ch: Friends, New York life and recording routine
95.q: Well, yeah, I always cooked for myself, because I always (unintelligible) sometimes wouldn't have nothing but a broiled steak, you know, and sometimes I had some rice and pork chops and something like that. I always would get a room where I could use the stove. I like mustard greens and corn bread…

95.t: Room rent and cooking a duck
95.s: She paid five or six dollars a week for a sleeping room and tells of ruining a duck by buttering it.
95.ch: Friends, New York life and recording routine
95.q: I remember one time, I had never cooked a duck and I was going to have a duck and I didn't know how to cook . I was so young. I didn't know how to cook no duck, so I had the duck and put it all full of butter. You don't butter no duck.

95.s: She liked New York but preferred Chicago because she knew more people there.
95.ch: Friends, New York life and recording routine
95.q: (Unintelligible). live in New York. I liked New York, but I liked Chicago, I think, better. Maybe it was because I knowed more people. 35.t: Moving to New York and staying with Kratka
35.s: Blumberg decides to move to New York at Kratka's urging, stays with the Kratkas, then gets a cheap room in the Village from Jan Kindler.
35.ch: Move to New York and the Stuyvesant
35.q: Well, Kratka was saying that I ought to move to New York. He wanted to get together this band he had in mind. So he invited me to stay at his family's place until I got a place of my own, and so I did move up. With my parents' permission this time, and stayed with the Kratkas, I guess, for several…

35.t: Hearing the second Stuyvesant band with Don Ewell
35.s: Blumberg dates his move to after the second Stuyvesant engagement and recalls Don's Jelly Roll style piano and Bunk taking more solos; Maude's presence is mentioned.
35.ch: Move to New York and the Stuyvesant
35.q: Yeah, well, of course, when I moved up to New York, I think the Stuyvesant engagement was over already. That ended about the 10th or so. Well, this was the second.

35.t: Bunk living with the Lofburrs and Freddie Moore, and the padlocked telephone
35.s: Bunk's New York residences, the padlock on Freddie Moore's wife's telephone, and Bunk idle and ignored in New York.
35.q: Well, he was living with the Lofburrs, as I recall, most of the time. There was also a period when he was living with... Who was it? Kaiser Marshall? Yeah. Kaiser Marshall's apartment, was it? No. No. The other drummer. Not Kaiser.

328.t: Leaving Indianapolis for New York via Cincinnati and Houston
328.s: After hearing Bud Powell at Birdland he set out with fifteen dollars, played with Miles in Cincinnati, spent a year in Houston and was taken to New York by Buddy Johnson.
328.ch: Road to New York and Maynard Ferguson
328.q: Well see when we played the Apollo Theater we had such success that the booking agents wanted us to stay in New York. And we would have had a good success in New York. But my sisters wanted to go back to Indianapolis. You know how ladies are. And so we didn’t stay. And after I was in New York the…

328.t: Why his siblings would not stay in New York
328.s: His brothers and sisters found New York too fast and returned to Indianapolis; Brower muses the family band was ahead of its time.
328.q: They felt that New York was fast. It was fast. They just didn’t have the desire to stay there. There were a lot of opportunities there. They wouldn’t stay.

328.t: Starving and practicing in a one-room kitchenette with Hubbard
328.s: Hampton shared a room across from the Apollo with Freddie Hubbard, Floyd Brady and Rocky Boyd, hungry but practicing.
328.ch: Maynard Ferguson and Dizzy's big band
328.q: Sometimes we weren’t working at all, because we were new. So we were there living – Freddie Hubbard, myself, and two other guys in a room. We weren’t working at all. We practiced all the time.

141.t: Why he moved to New York in 1956, and the colorful rustic label
141.s: Inspired by the jazz boom and tired of southern lounges, he resisted a promoter's pitch to play up his Mississippi roots.
141.ch: Baton Rouge, first New York trip, the road years
141.q: You played in San Antonio... You traveled all around the Gulf Coast. Then it’s 1956, and you get to New York. Here’s what you said about what finally decided you on moving. You said: “Dave Brubeck got on the cover of Time magazine in 1954,” and jazz is getting a certain amount of attention, the…

141.t: First New York apartment on 106th Street
141.s: The family lived in a furnished fourth-floor walk-up for $150 a month.
141.q: Not Central Park West. It was between Columbus and Amsterdam. In fact, it was 106th Street. That fourth floor walk-up we lived in was on 106th Street between Columbus and Amsterdam. I know, because went to work every morning.

141.t: Deciding to go to New York; saving $800 at a Florida racetrack club
141.s: With a baby, he had to test New York or sell shoes; two football players' club in Florida let them save $800.
141.ch: Baton Rouge, first New York trip, the road years
141.q: No. Or HE would have to do it. Which meant there was no way we were just going to New York. I guess in there... Is there something about when you worked at the club that those two football players started, and that’s where we saved $800 to come to New York.

1.t: Uncle Paul sends for him to come to New York
1.s: With the Depression biting, Paul Barbarin offered him a ticket, and Barker talks about how New Orleans lacked publishing know-how.
1.ch: Professional start and leaving New Orleans
1.q: Oh, yeah. My uncle . . . The Depression set in 1929. The Depression set, and there was no work here. People don’t have no [? (inaudible)] ain’t no work. So he wrote down here. He’s my godfather, and he’s interested in me, because he know I had ambition. He said, “Why don’t you come up to New York?”…

1.t: Arriving at Pennsylvania Station with a banjo
1.s: Paul Barbarin and Red Allen met him and rushed him through the New York crowd at Pennsylvania Station.
1.q: Yeah and they’re running. Them bulls is behind them. That’s the kind of scene that was to me. I said, “[expletive deleted], I’ll miss it.” “Come on through.” I said, “Uh­ uh, man.” Finally, they got through, and they grabbed me by the hand and drug me through all them people, boy. The people just…

1.t: Moving to New York in 1930 and feeding the musicians
1.s: Lu joined Danny a month after he went to New York, and she cooked for the many musicians Danny brought home.
1.ch: Lu Barker and the Barbarin family
1.q: Mmm-hmm. Now, I didn't like to wash dishes. So he'd tell them, "Well, man, I'll bring you to eat, but you've got to wash the plates." Because I told them I was tired of washing all them dishes now. They could eat, but they'd have to wash the dishes. Anybody Danny met, he'd tell them to come to my…

490.t: Detroit musicians who followed him to New York
490.s: Everyone who left Detroit with him succeeded in New York, and he had a reputation before arriving.
490.ch: Charlie Parker, dances and house parties
490.q: Yeah, well what it is, is all the musicians that left with me, they all made it in New York. Every musician, I don’t know any one that didn’t, you know. Um, what’s the pianist’s name at Arturo? Um, Richard – the pianist at Arturo’s? No, the regular pianist that played for the singers and stuff

490.t: New York trips, Art Blakey, and hibernating from 1960
490.s: He first visited New York in the early 1950s, sat in with Art Blakey, then joined Cannonball and settled near the Staten Island Ferry in 1960.
490.q: Oh, thank you. Um, let’s see.

490.t: First trip to New York and Sheila Jordan's Hamtramck story
490.s: He went to New York around 1952 with Doug Watkins, and tells how Sheila Jordan nearly got him beaten up in a Hamtramck bar.
490.q: See, I left out a whole lot of people, though. I left out Sheila Jordan, you know. I left out Skeeter, you know these are people who are all important to me. And when I went to New York for the first time – me and Doug went together, we stayed with Sheila Jordan, you know. Um, ‘cause Sheila Jordan…

526.t: Driving east with a boy and the records that drew her to Cafe Bohemia
526.s: She came east in a boy's car, stopped in Boston, wanted only to reach Cafe Bohemia, then moved in with Paul Bley and listened to jazz radio.
526.q: Oh that was a boy. But we didn’t have sex. He just didn’t want to. And we would neck for awhile and then he’d go to the front seat of the car and I’d stay in the back seat of the car and we went all the way like that to New York and went to his house in Boston. His father was the concertmaster of…

526.t: Arriving in New York, homeless, then cigarette girl at Birdland
526.s: She had no one in New York, slept in Grand Central, lived with a boyfriend, then worked as a cigarette girl at Birdland and Basin Street East where she met Paul Bley.
526.q: I went to New York. I had nobody there, I had to sleep in Grand Central Station on a bench. I fell in with some other homeless people and we would go crash at different people’s pads. And some of us were mentally ill, and would have fits during the night, all kinds of things. And I was just totally…

526.t: How Paul Bley noticed her and made her write
526.s: He bought cigarettes from her after she shushed customers during solos; she could not earn enough tips to return to Oakland.
526.q: Because I would never sell any cigarettes, I’d sit down there with the tray around my neck, and if someone asked me for a pack of Lucky’s I’d say “Are you crazy? Shhh! You have to be quiet until the solo’s over.”

470.t: Living in Los Angeles and in Harlem with Slide Hampton

470.ch: Cities, books, teaching, family and legacy

I ran into people like Gerald Wilson and friends that I would have had there. So it was valuable from the standpoint that I was in a…

470.t: Second New York stay with the Russell band

I already had a job. But I played sessions, I went again to the Café Wa, I went to clubs down in Greenwich Village and…

86.t: Following his girlfriend to New York

Uh and then I worked with Babatunde Olatunji for a while...’60 and ’61. And then in ’62 I worked with [Julian] “Cannonball” [Adderley] for two years. That was the…

137.t: Leaving Moten and going to New York to Willie Bryant
137.s: He left four weeks before Moten died, wanting something bigger, and went to New York at Bryant's request, where union transfer rules limited his playing.
137.q: Well, I was kind of a rolling stone, you know? Like, after you play with a band so long, I say, man, this band is at a standstill, I want to find something bigger and more exciting. I'd heard Duke Ellington, you know, and I wanted to leave because I said, the band has got all you need. Say, all…

26.t: Fats Waller needs a band and Greer takes Duke and others to New York
26.s: Fats Waller asks Greer for five musicians; Greer recruits Duke, Otto, Whetsol and Snowden, boasts of knowing New York and the Clef Club.
26.q: You know, so I go my way and have me some fun. I ain't paying anybody no mind. Because I'm way up on the hog, I'm making money. Pockets just laughing. And I wasn't married or nothing like that. I didn't know my wife existed then, anyway, Fats Waller came to town. I had been down there and I stayed…

379.t: Azpiazu's arrival and the friendship with Machin
379.s: He says he came on the same boat as Azpiazu and mentions his close friend Antonio Machin, linking to his later trumpet playing.
379.q: Yeah, I remember it was -- the front of it was a shinga (phonetic). They just pass away, man, and in Spain, [Antonio] MACHIN, the pay machine (phonetic) was a close friend of mine. So that's how I came to be a trumpet player, after I (inaudible). Later on I became a trumpet player.

28.t: First night in Harlem: Myra Johnson and the strange rooming house
28.s: Singer Myra Johnson protected the eighteen-year-old and put him up in a house where he was alone and frightened, and he left after two weeks.
28.ch: Newark and first years in Harlem
28.q: I say, 'I want to come in.' (Unintelligible)/ Yeah, how old are you? 18, sir. Now, wait now, and then Teddy Hill saw me and he said come on in here, man and (unintelligible) June Clark said yes, and I sit down and that waiter come over wiping the table, see those waiters can wipe those tables, you…

380.t: New York as home and returning to California
380.s: His parents moved to New York, but after a short stay with family in Brooklyn he knew California was where he belonged.
380.ch: Youth, the road and arrival in California
380.q: New York was like home, because my mother and dad had moved to New York -- and so I considered New York home. So I went back to New York... I still have family living in Brooklyn, incidentally; they've been in the same house for forty years. So I went back to New York, and I stayed with the family…

758.t: Leaving for New York, and the childhood visit
758.s: He sold the car in Indianapolis, went home and then to New York, where he had first been as a kid around 1925-26.
758.q: : I went to Indianapolis. I went to Indianapolis, sold the car, and went home to Pittsburgh. From Pittsburgh I took the train or the bus or something, and went to New York.

69.t: The ship Catalina and first impressions of New York
69.s: He recalls the ship, losing his money gambling, being overwhelmed by New York and eating family food rather than hearing any music.
69.ch: Arriving in America and the Howard Theatre
69.q: Oh, yeah, a regular ship. They used to leave every Wednesday for New York, and other boats used to leave for New York. Oh, it's a lot of trouble at that particular time, and there were no airplanes then to travel in.

120.t: A patron finances his move to New York
120.s: A generous woman who tips well at Blatt's Palm Gardens pays for his trip and car; he sorts out whether he left in 1940 or 1941 and finally gets Nick's.
120.ch: New York, Nick's and the Army
120.q: no names at this point -- but she was very interested in my career and she said to me once -- I was working at Blatt's Palm Gardens and she happened to be there-- and we played her favorite songs everytime she came in because she was a very good tipper and she once said to me, Bill, what is the…

232.t: The band's loyalty and Rozelle Claxton's ultimatum
232.s: The men say they will follow him back home; Rozelle Claxton says he will take Eddie South's offer if the band leaves.
232.ch: Melvin Moore, Hammond and the New York trip
232.q: And so I went on and I talked to the guys about it and as I told you, Chief had tried out with the band, and there's nothing that would do he, he had to leave town with us; so you know, the reputation has been known that bands come from the midwest or west or south, or anywhere, they're known to…

234.t: The West Beth loft: noise, a rooftop room and a martial-arts class
234.s: Gil talks about neighbors complaining about the sound and the idea of sharing a rooftop room with a martial arts teacher.
234.q: Except It's just that the sound there is a problem, as far as the neighbors are concerned, you know. Because the apartments are divided up into, the one we have for example has been one giant room at one time. So it's been divided up and (?).

92.t: Auditioning for Fletcher Henderson without saying who he was
92.s: After his mother's death he moved to New York in 1940 and won the Henderson guitar job without revealing that Henderson knew his mother, telling him six months later on a bus in Mississippi.
92.ch: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
92.q: Yeah, he said, but I'm over age. But any way, I never was -- I never tried to play like Charlie, still don't. But now, I told you that I was with Fletcher Henderson. I went to New York -- after my mother died I went to New York to live, 1938, '39, some time ago, '40. 1940. I had been to New York…

94.t: Living in Harlem with the Spratley family
94.s: Between Ernie Fields and Newark he lived on 118th Street with the Spratleys, kin to a drummer he knew.
94.ch: New York, Dallas and Kansas City
94.q: No, this comes later. I did join Ernie because he played the Apollo Theater. When my job ran out in Newark, I moved back into Harlem.

72.t: First lodgings and impressions of New York
72.s: He roomed on 129th Street for eight dollars a week and says New York lived up to what he was told.
72.q: I stayed at a place on 129th Street, a private house. I was paying about eight dollars a week for a room. I had a few dollars when I came here.

418.t: Coming to New York, McKinney's Cotton Pickers and Don Redman
418.s: Bands were not made until they came to New York; McKinney's Cotton Pickers came to record, and Don Redman wrote many songs.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: Well, they said you're not made until you come to New York in them days. I don't know if they still say that yet. I think they do.

386.t: Leaving Detroit for New York in 1937
386.s: After a 'female problem' he moves on, stops in Cleveland, and arrives to see stars outside 2040 Seventh Avenue.
386.ch: New York, Philadelphia and Harlem nightlife
386.q: Yeah, whenever I have a female problem (laughter), I always move on. Like Jimmy Shine, I will pack my clothes and move on down the line (laughter). I had a problem in Detroit, female problem, So I decided to come to New York, you know, to move to New York. And usually when I made those decisions…

148.t: Cut loose from the band and drifting to New York
148.s: The Raeburn years were fun with later knotted stomachs; Handy went home and then to New York, where trouble began.
148.q: Well you're being helpful to me. It's not easy to talk about those times, really. Those were very important times for me.

19.s: Eckstine wires asking him and Tommy Potter to join a new band in New York, and Malachi replies he is on his way.
19.ch: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
19.q: Anyway, I came on out. After I was home about a week, a couple of weeks... I don't even know how the news got to New York, but I got this telegram that I still have now, that said

427.t: Hammond's weekly money and Turner's homesickness in New York
427.s: Hammond gave him $500 a week to enjoy New York, and he grew homesick while others left for California.
427.q: Anyway, when I went to New York...well, when I left New York, went back to Kansas City...everybody said, "Oh, you couldn't make it... too rough for you." But I had told John Hammond that I was gettin' homesick. John Hammond used to give me five hundred dollars a week--work or no work--said, "Now,…

73.t: Arriving at his aunt's apartment in the Sixties
73.s: He describes his aunt's rooms off the West Sixties and who stayed with them.
73.q: Right. Right. She came up. And, she had, like a -- let me see if I can remember the story -- she had either two rooms and a kitchen. Something like that. But, anyway, I think she stayed there with us.

149.t: Earl Hines, Joe Glaser and choosing New York over Chicago
149.s: Hines heard Hawkins at 'Bama State and told Joe Glaser, who offered a ticket; on his aunt's advice Hawkins went to New York and got a break at the Harlem Opera House.
149.q: Right. I, oh yeah. I was in 'Bama State then. Earl Hines came down with his band to play a concert on the campus and I was in school then. And, we each would alternate. We did that with all the bands that came there.

389.t: Trumbauer's ambitions and the Red Nichols example
389.s: Trumbauer wanted to lead and record in New York as Red Nichols did and wanted Challis as arranger.
389.ch: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
389.q: Now he started the band all that time, and when we got to New York -- I didn't get into this politics, you know, I didn't know what it was all about because it went back further than I knew anything about. Now, Trumbauer had his own band and I think he was ambitious to be a leader and

81.t: Starting in New York and its heyday
81.s: He came to New York after leaving Chicago and has been there since; Rasch calls it the center of everything and he says he was on his way in the 1940s.
81.ch: Porch interview and Jazz Train plans
81.q: Yes. I came to New York, when I left home, in Chicago, and I've been in New York ever since.

76.t: Driving to New York with fifty cents and Wellman Braud's help
76.s: They drove east in a new Ford, ate salted peanuts and arrived in Harlem with fifty cents; Wellman Braud fed them and found a room at Miss Cotton's, the House of Meditation.
76.q: And we were hungry because we'd eaten, had a bag of salted peanuts and we ate that I think all the way from Philadelphia to New York or Pittsburg. We went to Pittsburg, that was our last stop, looking for Charlie. Didn't find, couldn't find him. My brother.

125.t: Taking a pay cut to join Lester in New York for love of the music
125.s: He left $75 a week with George Clarke's band to join Lester Young for $55, mainly for the music and because New York was a jazz mecca.
125.ch: New York with Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins
125.q: Yes, it was. Well, the fact of the matter is I'll tell you the strange thing about it is I was influenced to come there because of my love for music strictly,

239.t: Joining the Stuff Smith Trio and being talked into New York
239.s: John Levy writes to Jones, then working outside Chicago with Johnnie Board, to join Stuff Smith's violin-piano-bass trio and move to New York.
239.ch: Stuff Smith Trio and New York
239.q: Yes. That was a great experience. In fact it really triggered me off and triggered John Levy off in New York, because at the time in Chicago we'd made a pretty nice reputation, and we were getting good reviews and so consequently when we got to New York, everybody on opening night was in the house.…
